Examples: Six years ago, I got laid off, was living in my parent’s basement, and felt at one of the lowest points of my life.

Then, my friend @bee_sco13 sent me an app called “TikTok”, and while most people saw it as entertainment, I saw it as a creative outlet. The same spark I’d had my whole life.

In middle school, I had a Sony camera glued to me, writing scripts, bribing friends with snacks to act in my projects, editing late into the night, and showing my work to anyone who would watch. Even in high school and college, I was always “the kid who made videos.”

But I never thought I could make a career out of it. Coming from an immigrant family who sacrificed EVERYTHING for me, I knew I had more to prove and fewer risks I could take. So, I majored in Finance, focused on internships, and studied the stock market so intensely that it started to drain my creativity. I always knew I had to work harder than everyone else, and that immigrant-mindset hustle is what set me up for success.

Fast forward to 2020: I started making TikTok videos about what I knew best—brunch. I gained followers fast, brands started reaching out, people recognized me on the street—but I still didn’t fully see my own value. For three years, it felt like I had two jobs, until content finally outpaced my corporate career.

I left my corporate job in 2023. Since then, I’ve doubled my salary, become my own boss, interviewed the mayor of NYC, worked with dream brands, and hit milestones I never imagined—proving my passion was my purpose all along.

The main lesson I learned from all this, is that you should never stop doing what you love, because if you are consistent with it, it will eventually pay off. 

I am so proud to say that the younger version of me would be screaming, in tears, if he knew where I am today: a full-time content creator making videos about myself, about who I am, about what I love… and people actually care to watch?! Shut up.

Improve your basic latte art patterns by RE-pouring technique.
Pour your first cup back to the jug, 
pour some of the mixed milk in the cup, 
sprinkle with cacao powder, 
and so on until the milk is too watery.
This is one of the most effective and efficient ways to practice and strengthen your basic latte art pattern.
For well frothed fresh milk, it can be re-pour up 8-10x normal speed like in the video.
.
.
Preparation:
1. French press,
Am using bodum 350ml
2. Fresh milk, adjust with your cup capacity. 
Am using 6oz Chliv cup. 
So I prepare 180ml
3. Microwave/common stove will do, to heat the milk up to 55-65 degrees celcius
4. Instant coffee, 1-2gr + 15ml water as base
5. Cacao powder for a better contrast canvas in the RE-pouring cup

FRENCH PRESS FROTHING GUIDE for silky milk texture to pour basic latte art pattern

1. 4x big pumps 
• milk streching 
• pump from above the surface to very bottom
• slow speed

2. 10-15x near surface submerged pumps
• induce more air 
• add volume to milk 
• approx 1-2cm up from the non frothed milk before pumping
• submerged pump from bottom up to near but not above the surface 
• medium speed

3. 40-60x bottom submerged pumps
• break big bubbles
• mix in and distribute evenly the air
• form a silky texture 
• submerged pump from bottom to the middle milk volume
• fast speed 

NOTES
Manual frothing consists many variable factors,
So do your own trial and error to achieve a better milk texture that suit your pouring style.
